passage:
Naveen: why did you wave me off in the canteen yesterday
Naveen: like a fly 😅
Farhan: wait what
Naveen: you did this with your hand, palm out, shoo shoo
Farhan: OH. I was carrying a full tray of hot rasam and you were right behind me
Farhan: I meant 'give me a bit of space', not 'go away'
Naveen: I thought you were fed up with me
Farhan: no no. I should've said 'one sec, hot tray!'
Naveen: yes please, use words
Farhan: deal. the hand is for trays, not for you
Naveen: 😄 ok. lunch tomorrow?
Farhan: yes. I'll carry the rasam, you hold the door

qa.q: What was Farhan carrying when the hand went out?
qa.a: Farhan was carrying a full tray of hot rasam.

qa.q: What did Naveen think Farhan's wave meant, and what was Farhan feeling?
qa.a: Naveen thought Farhan was fed up with Naveen. Farhan actually felt crowded by the hot tray and only wanted space.

qa.q: What could Farhan say next time instead of waving?
qa.a: Farhan can say, "one sec, hot tray!" A few words show whether the wave means not now, give me air, or stay away.

qa.q: How might Naveen have felt after being waved off?
qa.a: Naveen probably felt brushed aside and worried about the friendship, which is why the question came. Hearing the reason let Naveen relax and joke.

grounding: A teenager's move-back hand wave is read as rejection but only meant space, and words clarify.

passage: At the crowded bus door in Pipli, Wasim pushed his palm out toward Suraj. "Back, back." Suraj stepped away, stung. Two aunties nearby waved their hands even harder at the people behind them, and nobody seemed offended. On the bus, Wasim saw Suraj sitting stiffly. "You okay?" "You waved me off like I was a stray goat." Wasim winced. "Sorry. My arm was squashed and I couldn't breathe. I only wanted a little air, not for you to go away." Suraj's shoulders eased. "Then just say 'thoda peeche'." Wasim laughed. "Thoda peeche, yaar. Done."

qa.q: In which place did Wasim push his palm out?
qa.a: At the crowded bus door in Pipli.

qa.q: What was Suraj feeling when Wasim waved Suraj back, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Suraj felt stung and possibly insulted, and sat stiffly on the bus. Suraj also compared it to being waved off like a stray goat.

qa.q: What could Wasim do next time he needs space?
qa.a: He can add words like 'thoda peeche' with the wave. A verbal follow-up clarifies without shaming anyone.

qa.q: Why might the aunties react differently to the same wave?
qa.a: People differ on how blunt a hand wave is, and in a crowd it is common. The aunties may see it as normal, while Suraj took it personally.

grounding: A teenager's move-back gesture can mean give me air rather than stay away, and words clarify.

subtype: Palm out as boundary in arguments [Regulating]
passage: In the small shop behind the tea stall, Tanuja's sister Zeenat was in full flow about the cricket match, then the neighbour, then the missing scissors. Tanuja had a exam paper to check. She raised her palm. "Give me a second." Zeenat stopped mid-word, mouth open. Tanuja closed her eyes, breathed, and said, "I'm not saying you're wrong. I just can't listen and think at once. Tell me in ten minutes?" Zeenat pressed her lips together. "Fine. But you didn't have to do the hand." "I know. Sorry. It was the words that mattered." She passed Zeenat a biscuit.

qa.q: What was Zeenat talking about when Tanuja raised her palm?
qa.a: Zeenat was talking about the cricket match, the neighbour and the missing scissors.

qa.q: What did Tanuja mean by raising her palm, and what was she feeling?
qa.a: She meant she needed a moment because she couldn't listen and think together. She felt overloaded, not angry at Zeenat.

qa.q: What could Tanuja do next time to keep respect intact?
qa.a: She can say a few words like "give me a second" as she raises her hand, and offer a time to talk later. That protects her boundary without sounding dismissive.

qa.q: How might Zeenat have felt when the palm went up?
qa.a: She felt cut off and a little dismissed, which is why she complained about the hand. Tanuja's explanation and apology eased it.

grounding: A teenager raises a palm to stop a sibling mid-rant, and adds words so the boundary stays respectful.

subtype: Palm out as boundary in arguments [Regulating]
passage: Kaito was halfway through a maths problem when Clara started her long rant about the school trip. He held up a palm without a word. Clara froze. "Seriously?" she said. "You're shutting me down?" Kaito took off his headphones. "No. Sorry. Give me a second, I lost my place." He finished the line, then turned around. "Okay. Go." Clara folded her arms, still stiff. "That hand looked like 'talk to the hand'." "I get that. I disagree with parts of your plan, though, and I wanted to listen properly." She sat on the desk edge. "Then listen properly."

qa.q: What was Kaito doing when Clara started her rant?
qa.a: He was halfway through a maths problem.

qa.q: What was Clara feeling when Kaito held up his palm?
qa.a: She felt shut down and dismissed, and her folded arms and stiff voice show it. Kaito's actual reason was that he needed a moment.

qa.q: What would you advise Kaito about using the palm?
qa.a: He can pair it with words like "give me a second" so it reads as a pause and not a brush-off. That keeps the respect.

qa.q: How does Kaito see the situation compared to Clara?
qa.a: He wanted to finish his thought so he could listen properly, and he disagrees with parts of her plan. She only saw the hand.

grounding: A teenager raises a palm mid-rant to say he needs a moment, and it can read as dismissive without words.

passage: Rajni, before you leave for the school exchange, listen. I'm Jasleen, and at fifteen, I visited a hill town with my class and asked a shopkeeper the way to the post office. He never lifted his hand. He pushed out his lips toward the left. I thought he was ignoring me and asked again, louder, and he did it again! Our guide laughed and told me lips or chin can be pointing. Later I pointed at a temple with my whole hand and an old woman frowned, because in her village people used a chin nod. Now I always add words: "Left at the tea stall?" and check.

qa.q: Where did Jasleen ask the way to the post office?
qa.a: Jasleen asked a shopkeeper in a hill town.

qa.q: What was Jasleen feeling when the shopkeeper pushed his lips out, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Jasleen felt confused and slightly annoyed, thinking the shopkeeper was ignoring the question, so Jasleen asked again louder. The shopkeeper was actually pointing.

qa.q: What could a traveller do to avoid mixing up gestures?
qa.a: Pair the gesture with words and check understanding, such as asking "Left at the tea stall?" That helps when styles vary by region.

qa.q: How might the old woman have seen Jasleen's pointing?
qa.a: She frowned because a whole-hand point felt rude in her village, where people used a chin nod. It was a difference of custom, not bad intent.

grounding: A teenager finds that pointing with lips, chin or whole hand differs by region, and pairs the gesture with words.

passage: The rain was pouring and the last bus to Madurai left in six minutes. Kamal ran into a tea shop and shouted, "Which way to the bus stand?" The owner didn't speak. He lifted his chin toward the street. Kamal looked at him, puzzled, then at the door. Nothing. His cousin Rukmini tugged his sleeve. "He's pointing with his chin, that way, left." Kamal asked, "Left at the tea stall, then straight?" The owner nodded and said, "Haan, left." They sprinted, splashing, and reached the bus stand just as the engine started.

qa.q: How many minutes were left until the last bus left?
qa.a: The last bus to Madurai left in six minutes.

qa.q: What was Kamal feeling when the owner lifted his chin without speaking?
qa.a: He felt puzzled and pressed for time, since he stared at the shopkeeper and then the door. He didn't recognise the chin as a pointing gesture.

qa.q: What worked when the gesture was unclear?
qa.a: Rukmini explained it and Kamal checked with a spoken question. Pairing words with the gesture confirmed the way.

qa.q: How might the tea shop owner have seen Kamal's confusion?
qa.a: He probably thought a chin point was clear enough and didn't realise it looked odd to Kamal. Once asked in words, he answered clearly.

grounding: A teenager meets chin pointing, which is confusing elsewhere, and checks understanding in words under time pressure.

passage: The school bus was packed and noisy, with the monsoon drumming on the roof, but Nirmala had to tell Tenzin about the last-minute goal. Both her arms flew out wide. "The ball came in like this, fast, then whoosh!" Her elbow hit the seat in front, and the boy sitting there groaned and laughed. Tenzin, grinning, leaned forward so he could hear. Later, after a long day, Nirmala told him about a small prank in the staff room with her hands barely leaving her lap. Tenzin noticed. "You're a lot quieter this time. Tired?" "Very," she said, and yawned. "Tell me tomorrow."

qa.q: What was hitting the roof of the school bus?
qa.a: The monsoon was drumming on the roof.

qa.q: What did Nirmala's big sweeping arms suggest, and what might her small hands later suggest?
qa.a: The big gestures show excitement about the goal. Her small hands later may mean tiredness, which she confirmed by yawning.

qa.q: What could Tenzin do when a friend's story gets quieter?
qa.a: He can gently ask if they're tired and let them tell it another day, as he did. Reading gesture size is a cue, not proof.

qa.q: How might the boy in the seat in front have felt when Nirmala's elbow hit it?
qa.a: He groaned but laughed, so he took it as part of her excited storytelling. A different person might have been annoyed.

grounding: A teenager tells a match story with wide sweeping gestures showing excitement, and small gestures later show tiredness.

passage: In the colony park, Neelam described the frog she'd hidden in her cousin's school bag, with arms stretched wide, hopping motions, and a shriek for the finale. Swati laughed until she had to sit down. When it was Swati's turn to describe the prank the frog got back, her hands stayed close to her chest, tapping quietly. But her eyes were shining and her words tumbled fast. Neelam said, "You've hardly moved your hands, but you look thrilled." Swati smiled. "At home, big hands mean loud, and Nani doesn't like loud. It's just how I tell stories."

qa.q: Where did Neelam tell the story about the frog?
qa.a: She told it in the colony park.

qa.q: What does Swati's small hand movement mean, given her shining eyes?
qa.a: It doesn't mean she's bored, since she looks thrilled. Her habit of small gestures comes from home, where big hands mean loud.

qa.q: What might Neelam keep in mind when a friend's gestures look small?
qa.a: Small hands can come from culture or habit, not lack of interest. She can look at the eyes and speed of words too, and ask.

qa.q: How might Swati see Neelam's wide gestures?
qa.a: She probably finds them fun and full of drama, but different from what is normal at home. She laughed so hard she had to sit down.

grounding: A teenager tells a prank with hands, and gesture size shows excitement or is shaped by culture, so small hands need not mean reluctance.

passage: Tenzin, come and sit. Fifty years ago I had my interview for the teachers' college, and my knees were water. The night before, my brother Dorje asked me question after question until I could answer in my sleep. That morning, in the corridor, I remembered what my headmistress told me: stand tall, shoulders back, take one good breath. I did. It didn't make the nerves vanish, but it steadied my voice. Still, what really got me through was knowing my subject, because I had practised. A straight back helps, but you can't stand your way out of not knowing. That was me, Tenzin, your Nani Nirmala.

qa.q: What did Nirmala's brother do the night before her interview?
qa.a: Her brother Dorje asked her question after question.

qa.q: What was Nirmala feeling in the corridor, and what helped her?
qa.a: She was nervous, with knees like water, and standing tall with a good breath steadied her. She says the preparation mattered most.

qa.q: Which choice before the interview helped Nirmala most, and why?
qa.a: Practising with Dorje the night before helped most, because knowing her subject carried her; standing tall and breathing only steadied her voice.

qa.q: How might Dorje's help have felt for Nirmala?
qa.a: It probably made her feel supported and gave her real answers to rely on. His questions did more than a power pose could.

grounding: A teenager preparing for an interview stands straight and breathes to calm nerves, but relies on preparation.

passage: The rain had made Arnab twenty minutes late for the scholarship interview, and the waiting room was full. His aunt Kalyani had practised mock questions with him all week, but his heart was banging. He stood by the door, feet apart, and straightened his back. One slow breath in. A longer one out. He wasn't feeling brave, exactly, but steadier. When the panel called his name, he walked in and shook hands. He stumbled on the first question. Then the answers Kalyani had drilled came back, and he found his rhythm. Afterwards he told her, "The breathing helped. But the practice helped more."

qa.q: How late was Arnab because of the rain?
qa.a: He was twenty minutes late.

qa.q: What was Arnab feeling by the door, and what helped?
qa.a: His heart was banging, so he was anxious. Standing straight and taking slow breaths steadied him, and the drilled answers gave him confidence.

qa.q: What should Arnab remember for future interviews?
qa.a: Stand straight and breathe to calm nerves, but keep preparing with practice questions. Preparation carries the real weight.

qa.q: How might Kalyani have felt hearing his words afterwards?
qa.a: She probably felt glad that her mock questions helped and that he noticed. His thanks credits the practice.

grounding: A teenager before an interview stands straight and breathes, and credits preparation most.

subtype: Slumping and crossing arms as protection [Regulating]
passage: "Sit up, Shreya, don't look so rude," said Manjula, coming into the living room. Shreya was slumped on the sofa, knees drawn up, arms crossed tight. From the next room came her parents' raised voices. Manjula stopped. "Is it cold in here, or is it the noise?" "The noise," whispered Shreya. "I make myself small so it doesn't get me." "Ah, Masi understands." Manjula sat next to her, not too close. "I'm not sitting up for you. Want some tea and to tell me about it, or just sit here?" "Just sit," Shreya said. They sat.

qa.q: Where was Shreya slumped?
qa.a: She was slumped on the sofa in the living room.

qa.q: What was Shreya feeling when she crossed her arms and drew up her knees?
qa.a: She felt anxious and wanted to feel smaller and safer, because the raised voices upset her. She says she makes herself small so the noise doesn't get her.

qa.q: How could Manjula support Shreya?
qa.a: She can ask gently how Shreya feels and offer a choice to talk or just sit. She avoids commenting on manners.

qa.q: How does Manjula's view of the crossed arms change?
qa.a: At first she read it as rude and told Shreya to sit up. Then she asked a question and saw it was protection.

grounding: A teenager slumps and crosses arms in a tense home to feel smaller and safer, and an adult reads it kindly.

subtype: Slumping and crossing arms as protection [Regulating]
passage: I'm Bidisha. In my local train to college, I always fold myself into a corner, shoulders hunched and arms crossed tight. Someone once said I looked rude, like I didn't want anyone near. Actually the carriage is so packed that I feel like I'm being swallowed, and tucking in makes me feel a little safer. Last week Lakshmi, a girl from my class, stood next to me and asked, "You okay? You look like you're bracing." No one had asked that before. I said, "It's just crowded." She said, "Want to swap and take the corner spot? I don't mind." We swapped, and I breathed a little easier.

qa.q: Where does Bidisha fold into a corner?
qa.a: In the local train to college.

qa.q: What is Bidisha feeling when hunching and crossing both arms?
qa.a: Bidisha feels swallowed by the crowd and is trying to feel safer. It looks rude to some, but Bidisha says it protects.

qa.q: What small step helped Bidisha on the train?
qa.a: Lakshmi asked if Bidisha was okay and offered to swap places. A kind question and a practical offer helped.

qa.q: How might Lakshmi have read Bidisha's posture?
qa.a: Lakshmi saw someone bracing, not rude, and asked instead of judging. She read it as tension in a crowd.

grounding: A teenager slumps and crosses arms in a crowd to feel safer, and a classmate reads it as protection, not rudeness.

passage:
Hemant: are you doing the group dance at the function
Omkar: yes!! but my palms are sweaty already 😅
Hemant: you love it though
Omkar: I do. when we all move together I feel like I belong, you know?
Hemant: yeah I get that
Omkar: but Kabir said I should skip it because 'boys don't do that'
Hemant: did that change your mind
Omkar: it made me feel a bit small for a day
Omkar: then I thought no. it's my choice
Hemant: good. I'll stand at the back and clap for you
Omkar: come on the stage
Hemant: ...ok fine, I'll dance badly 🙂

qa.q: Which event is Omkar going to dance at?
qa.a: Omkar is going to dance at the function.

qa.q: What is Omkar feeling about the dance, and what mixed feelings show?
qa.a: Omkar feels joy and belonging when they move together, and some nerves too, since the palms are sweaty. Omkar felt small after Kabir's remark before deciding it was a personal choice.

qa.q: What could Omkar do if someone teases about dancing?
qa.a: Omkar can remember it's a personal choice and lean on friends who back the decision. Omkar can also tell a trusted adult if teasing turns unkind.

qa.q: How might Hemant feel about being asked onto the stage?
qa.a: Hemant seems shy about dancing but agrees to join Omkar. Choice matters for Hemant too.

grounding: A teenager dances in a group to show joy and belonging, and teasing shows why choice matters.

passage: The village wedding baraat came down the lane in a haze of dust and drums. Binita's cousins pulled her into the circle, and she found herself laughing and stepping in time, arms up, feet quick. She felt part of everything. Then Divyansh, watching from a scooter, called out, "Look at her moves, she's a film star!" in a teasing sing-song. Binita's steps faltered. Her face went hot and she slipped to the edge. Divyansh saw it and walked over. "Sorry, I only meant it as a joke. You looked great." After a while she stepped back in, at her own pace.

qa.q: How did the baraat come down the lane?
qa.a: It came down in a haze of dust and drums.

qa.q: What was Binita feeling as she danced, and after Divyansh's remark?
qa.a: She felt joy and belonging while dancing. After the teasing she felt embarrassed, as her steps faltered and her face went hot.

qa.q: What went right when Divyansh walked over?
qa.a: Divyansh apologised and said Binita looked great, which let Binita choose to dance again. Divyansh noticed the effect of the joke.

qa.q: How might Divyansh have seen Divyansh's own comment at first?
qa.a: Divyansh meant it as a friendly joke, and did not expect it to shame her. Seeing her go to the edge changed that.

grounding: A teenager dances at a wedding baraat for joy and belonging, and teasing can turn joy to shame while choice restores it.

subtype: Walking away as boundary or avoidance [Mismatch]
passage: At the school gate, three older boys started taunting Amandeep about his stammer. His jaw tightened. Without a word, he turned and walked off toward the library. Jatin, watching, felt confused. "He just ran away," a boy beside him said. Jatin wasn't sure. At the library, Amandeep sat, breathed, and stared at his hands. When Jatin came in, Amandeep said, "I needed a break, or I'd have said something I'd regret. I'm not scared. I'm going to tell Sir at the end of the day." Jatin sat beside him. "I'll come with you." Amandeep gave a small nod.

qa.q: Where did Amandeep walk after the boys taunted him?
qa.a: He walked toward the library.

qa.q: What was Amandeep feeling when he walked away?
qa.a: He was angry and hurt and needed a break so he wouldn't say something he'd regret. He also says he isn't scared, though his tight jaw shows tension.

qa.q: What small step made his walking away clear and trusted?
qa.a: He told Jatin he needed a break and would tell Sir later. Saying so shows it is de-escalation, not avoidance.

qa.q: How might the boy next to Jatin have read the walking away?
qa.a: He saw it as running away because he only saw the leaving. Without words, it can look like avoidance.

grounding: A teenager walks away from a taunt, which could be wise de-escalation, and saying it clarifies the meaning.

subtype: Walking away as boundary or avoidance [Mismatch]
passage:
"Ira, we're not finished," said Pema, as her sister left the kitchen mid-sentence.
"I'm going upstairs."
"You always walk off when it gets hard."
Ira stopped on the stairs. "Maybe. Or maybe I'm embarrassed and can't think."
"Embarrassed about the exam?"
"Yes. Give me a little while and I'll come back. Really."
Pema let out a breath. "Okay. Say it next time, so I don't think you're avoiding me."
"I will."
A little later Ira came down. "Ready. Sorry I went quiet. I'll tell you about the marks now."

qa.q: Where did Ira walk to when she left the kitchen?
qa.a: She walked upstairs.

qa.q: What was Ira feeling when she walked away, and what did she say?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and couldn't think, and asked for a break with a promise to return. Pema had read it as avoiding.

qa.q: What could Ira do so her walking away isn't misread?
qa.a: She can say she needs a little while and will come back before leaving, and then keep her word. That keeps trust.

qa.q: What is it like for Pema when Ira leaves mid-sentence?
qa.a: She feels that Ira avoids hard talks and may feel shut out. Ira's promise and return show it was a pause.

grounding: A teenager walks away from a hard talk, and saying she needs a little while and will return keeps trust.

passage: In the school yard in Ohio, a group of older students surrounded Tomas near the roof stairs. "Just climb up, it's a dare, everyone does it." Tomas stood stiff, eyes wide, unable to speak or move. One student said, "See? He's not saying no. He's fine." Mateo, passing with his bag, saw Tomas's frozen face and clenched hands. He walked over. "He's not fine. Silence isn't a yes." He turned to Tomas. "Come on, we're going to the office." Tomas followed, slowly finding his legs, and Mateo told the teacher what had happened. The teacher sat Tomas down, said, "You did nothing wrong by freezing," and went straight out to the yard to stop the group before the bell.

qa.q: Where did the older students surround Tomas?
qa.a: They surrounded him near the roof stairs.

qa.q: What was Tomas probably feeling when he stood stiff and could not speak?
qa.a: He was frightened and frozen by the pressure, and his wide eyes and clenched hands suggest fear. Freezing is a stress response and does not mean agreement.

qa.q: What did Mateo do that helped?
qa.a: He said silence isn't a yes, took Tomas away and told a teacher. Getting an adult was the right step.

qa.q: How might the student who said 'he's fine' have seen the stillness?
qa.a: They took the stillness as agreement to fit what they wanted. Stillness under pressure should never be read as a yes.

grounding: A teenager freezes when pressured, and others must never read stillness as consent.

passage: In the hostel corridor, Yamini's senior cornered her by the water cooler, demanding she join an 'initiation' that involved taking a bag from another room. "Everyone does it. Just say yes." Yamini stood without moving, her throat closed, her face blank. Vaibhav, another resident, came out of his room and saw her stillness and how her hands hung. He knew it wasn't agreement. "Yamini, are you okay? You don't have to do anything." She managed a tiny shake of her head. Vaibhav said, "Let's go to the warden," and walked her there, leaving the senior behind. The warden listened to both of them, told Yamini, "This is not your fault," and called the senior to the office that same evening.

qa.q: Where did the senior corner Yamini?
qa.a: The senior cornered her by the water cooler in the hostel corridor.

qa.q: What was Yamini feeling when she stood without moving and her throat closed?
qa.a: She was frightened and pressured, and froze. Her blank face and closed throat show fear, not consent.

qa.q: How could Vaibhav keep supporting Yamini after the warden steps in?
qa.a: Vaibhav can check on Yamini later, stay nearby if she wants company, and back up what he saw if the warden asks. Nobody should treat her silence as a yes.

qa.q: How might the senior have read Yamini's silence?
qa.a: The senior may have wrongly taken it as going along with it. Freezing is an involuntary stress response.

grounding: A teenager freezes when pressured, which is not consent, and a peer notices and gets an adult.

subtype: Shielding the body and avoiding notice [Mismatch]
passage: At the school function, Karthik sat at the end of the row with his sleeves pulled down over his hands, shoulders hunched, chin tucked. He'd just got braces that morning and didn't want anyone to see him smile. Asif noticed him hiding behind the programme sheet. He didn't tease. He sat beside Karthik and said quietly, "Rough day?" Karthik shrugged into his sleeves. "Braces." Asif nodded. "Fine by me. I'll save you a seat by the snacks." A small smile appeared under the sleeve, and Karthik lowered his hands, slowly.

qa.q: What did Karthik pull over his hands?
qa.a: He pulled his sleeves down over his hands.

qa.q: What was Karthik feeling as he hid behind the programme sheet?
qa.a: He was self-conscious about his new braces and afraid of being seen smiling. The hunched shoulders and tucked chin fit that, though it might also be something else.

qa.q: How could a friend help someone who is hiding like this?
qa.a: Sit nearby, don't tease, and accept them as they are, as Asif did. A quiet question is enough.

qa.q: How might Karthik have felt when Asif sat next to him without mocking?
qa.a: He probably felt relieved and accepted. The small smile under the sleeve suggests he began to relax.

grounding: A teenager pulls sleeves over hands and hunches when self-conscious, and steady acceptance helps.

subtype: Shielding the body and avoiding notice [Mismatch]
passage: "Karthik, why do you go all hunched every time Rohan walks by?" Sabina asked as they ate. "I don't." "You pulled your sleeves over your hands and looked at your shoes. Just now." Karthik was quiet. "He keeps calling me names in the corridor. When he's near I just want to disappear." Sabina put her fork down. "That isn't okay. Have you told anyone?" "No." "Would you tell Mrs. Nair? I'll come with you." Karthik took a shaky breath. "Okay. After lunch." In the staffroom Mrs. Nair listened to all of it. "Thank you for telling me, Karthik. This is not your fault. I'll speak to Rohan today, and you come and see me tomorrow morning."

qa.q: What does Karthik do when Rohan walks by?
qa.a: Karthik hunches, pulls sleeves over both hands and looks down at their shoes.

qa.q: What is Karthik feeling when Rohan is near?
qa.a: Karthik is uneasy and afraid of being seen, and wants to disappear, because Rohan keeps calling Karthik names.

qa.q: Which choice helped Karthik, and why?
qa.a: Telling Mrs. Nair that same day with Sabina beside them, because an adult can act on the name-calling and Karthik no longer has to hide alone.

qa.q: How might Sabina feel seeing Karthik hide?
qa.a: She may feel worried and protective, so she asks and offers to go along to the staffroom.

grounding: A teenager shields the body and avoids notice around one person, and a friend encourages telling a trusted adult.
